basis: eternal punitive death without extinction
note: Augustine argues that the damned can endure punitive death without being annihilated; this gives a Christian account of the continuing, non-living condition the commentary marks in 87:13.

basis: Paradise trees and no taste of death
note: The saying describes unchanging trees in Paradise and promises that those who know them will not taste death; this is a concrete apocryphal image of the immortality sought in the commentary's false tree offer, recast as a blessed promise.

basis: perishable body raised imperishable
note: Resurrection is sown perishable and raised imperishable; it gives a bodily account of the enduring life set over against death in the commentary.

basis: Mortality clothed with immortality
note: Paul's resurrection scene says the mortal must put on immortality and death is swallowed up in victory; it gives the hereafter's enduring life a concrete bodily endpoint unlike the fire's suspended condition.

basis: Hosea's death taunt in resurrection
note: Paul quotes the death-and-Sheol taunt associated with Hosea to celebrate resurrection's victory; this Christian reading turns the Hebrew prophet's ambiguous challenge into an assured defeat of death, unlike the commentary's unrelieved punishment.

basis: World passes, God's will remains
note: John says the world and its desire are passing, while the one who does God's will remains forever; this closely specifies the commentary's near worldly life versus the more enduring hereafter.

basis: world passes away, God-doer abides forever
note: The world and its desire are passing away, while the one who does God's will abides forever; this is a close formulation of transient worldly life against lasting life.

basis: Imperishable inheritance kept in heaven
note: Peter describes an inheritance in heaven that cannot perish, spoil, or fade; this specifies what enduring future good means beside the commentary's contrast with the near world.

basis: believers who sleep and hope beyond grief
note: Paul calls the deceased "those who sleep" and contrasts believers' grief with those without hope; this Christian death-as-sleep idiom supplies the recoverable horizon that the commentary denies to the fire-dweller.

basis: Taking hold of true life
note: After warning against trust in uncertain riches, Paul urges the rich to lay hold of “the life that is truly life”; this gives a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's distinction between mere worldly life and life as real benefit.

basis: future treasure and the life that is truly life
note: Generous use of wealth lays a foundation for the future so that one may grasp "the life that is truly life"; it is a pointed counterpart to choosing near worldly life over the enduring real life.

basis: Visible things pass, unseen things are eternal
note: Paul contrasts visible, temporary things with unseen, eternal things; this makes a concrete temporal-versus-enduring contrast for the commentary's worldly life and better hereafter.

basis: seen temporary, unseen eternal
note: The seen is temporary and the unseen eternal; its explicit temporal-eternal contrast supplies the evaluative frame of "better and more enduring" in 87:17.

basis: earthly tent and eternal heavenly house
note: The earthly tent is contrasted with an eternal house in the heavens not made by hands; the image maps present bodily life and a durable future dwelling onto the commentary's transient/enduring division.

basis: mortality swallowed up by life
note: Paul says that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life, a concise Christian expression of life overcoming mortality that illuminates the commentary's definition of true life as permanence.

basis: eternal destruction as punishment
note: The disobedient suffer "eternal destruction" away from the Lord; the wording gives a Christian punitive alternative to 87:13's unusual condition in which the condemned do not die, while leaving the meaning of destruction to be read in its own context.

basis: Life and immortality disclosed
note: Paul says Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality to light; this offers a Christian counter-image to the condemned person's unrelieved suspension between death and life.

basis: Jannes and Jambres oppose Moses
note: The letter names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses and compares false teachers to them; this Christian memory of the magicians reverses the commentary's scene of Pharaoh's magicians becoming faithful.

basis: sowing to flesh yields corruption, Spirit yields eternal life
note: Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; its present choice and later harvest closely match the commentary's worldly preference and enduring consequence.

basis: Abraham expects resurrection
note: Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise Isaac even from the dead; this is a Christian interpretation of the Abraham story that makes concrete the commentary's closing claim that God kills and then gives life.

basis: Abraham expects God to raise the dead
note: Hebrews reads Abraham's offering of Isaac through resurrection: he considers God able to raise even from the dead. That interpretation makes the commentary's Abrahamic death-and-life confession into a specific remembered test.

basis: Temporary pleasure refused
note: Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin; this is a specific counter-choice to the commentary's charge that people prefer the near life.

basis: temporary enjoyment versus suffering with God's people
note: Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin, a Pharaoh-linked Christian reading of a choice between passing advantage and a more durable divine horizon.

basis: Moses looks to the reward
note: Hebrews explains Moses' choice by his regard for a greater future reward; the commentary likewise ranks the hereafter above the present life and calls it more enduring.

basis: Egyptian riches set against a future reward
note: Moses considers reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; it separately supplies the Egypt-specific valuation of durable reward over near advantage developed in 87:16-17.

basis: torture refused for a better resurrection
note: Some are tortured and refuse release in order to obtain a better resurrection; this is a direct martyr-and-tyrant counterpart to the commentary's believing magicians facing Pharaoh's violence for a more lasting outcome.

basis: No lasting city here
note: Hebrews says believers have no lasting city here and seek the city to come; this gives a concrete formulation of present life as provisional beside the commentary's more enduring hereafter.

basis: no enduring city here, one to come
note: Believers have no lasting city here but seek the city to come, making the commentary's near-life and abiding-hereafter contrast spatial and communal.

basis: Life as a passing mist
note: James compares human life to a mist that appears briefly and vanishes; this makes the present life transitory beside the commentary's enduring hereafter, though it does not itself describe resurrection.

basis: life as a vapor that appears briefly
note: James calls present life a vapor appearing for a little while and vanishing, a concrete Christian account of the brevity implied by the commentary's name for the near life.

basis: sleep and promised awakening
note: Jesus calls Lazarus asleep and says that he will awaken him, a recoverable sleep-state set against the commentary's insistence that the fire offers neither sleep nor waking.

basis: Though dead, will live
note: Jesus says the believer who dies will live; this is a direct reversal of the commentary's “neither dies nor lives,” though it concerns the faithful and resurrection rather than punishment.

basis: one who dies will live
note: Jesus identifies himself as resurrection and life and promises life to the believer who dies; it supplies a concise Christian answer to the commentary's contrast between ordinary death and true enduring life.

basis: Believer will never die
note: Jesus adds that whoever lives and believes will never die; this supplies an affirmative, promised form of permanence in contrast to the commentary's barren non-life.

basis: Water springing to eternal life
note: Jesus describes water becoming a spring that wells up to eternal life; this connects the commentary's life-giving Paradise water with an image of water whose effect is enduring life.

basis: living water wells up to eternal life
note: Jesus promises water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life, making life-giving water an interior and enduring reality rather than merely a garden image.

basis: Father raises the dead and gives life
note: As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he wishes; this is a direct Christian articulation of death and life as divine acts.

basis: Passing from death into life
note: Jesus says the believer has passed from death into life and will not come into judgment; this is distinct from the future resurrection promise in John 11, presenting life as a present changed status rather than the commentary's condemned suspension.

basis: passing from death into life
note: The believer has passed from death into life and does not come into judgment, a compact Johannine two-destiny formulation beside 87:13's denied life in punishment.

basis: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
note: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food that endures to eternal life, directly framing a present material pursuit against an abiding life as the commentary does in 87:16-17.

basis: False security ended by death
note: The rich fool plans many years of ease from his stored goods, but his life is demanded that night; this concretely exposes the false permanence behind investment in worldly life.

basis: water requested in flame
note: The rich man in flame asks for a drop of water to cool his tongue; it sets a denied water-image inside punitive fire against the commentary's paradise water that confers life.

basis: Reversal after worldly comfort
note: Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in his lifetime while Lazarus received bad, but now Lazarus is comforted and the rich man suffers; this is a specific reversal of preferring present worldly ease over the afterlife.

basis: good things in lifetime, anguish after death
note: Abraham contrasts the rich man's good things in his lifetime with his present anguish and Lazarus's comfort; the story concretely tests the commentary's claim that preferring the near life ends in a radically different final condition.

basis: a fixed chasm prevents passage
note: The great chasm between the tormented rich man and Lazarus is fixed so that no one can cross; this continuation of the water-and-fire scene adds the commentary's concern with remaining in a condition without an exit.

basis: profit from the world and forfeiting one's life
note: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; the profit/life juxtaposition closely engages the commentary's claim that life includes benefit and its warning about choosing the worldly life.

basis: Enter life or Gehenna
note: Jesus contrasts entering life with being thrown into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; this connects the commentary's fire and negated life to an explicit choice between life and punishment.

basis: entering life versus Gehenna's unquenchable fire
note: Jesus contrasts entering life, even maimed, with being cast into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; it directly joins the commentary's two outcomes of real life and fire rather than merely naming punishment.

basis: Isaiah's worm applied to Gehenna
note: Mark places Isaiah's undying worm and unquenched fire in Jesus' warning about Gehenna; the Christian reuse shifts Isaiah's corpse image into a warning about final judgment, while still not saying the condemned themselves are alive.

basis: worm does not die and fire is not quenched
note: Mark reapplies the Isaiah image within Jesus' Gehenna teaching: the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. It supplies a Christian continuation of the deathless, unextinguished fire imagery, while the undying subject remains the worm rather than the punished person.

basis: body and soul destroyed in Gehenna
note: Jesus distinguishes human killing of the body from God's ability to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna; this provides a concrete Christian counter-formula to the commentary's fire in which the condemned do not die.

basis: Losing life to find it
note: Jesus says the one who seeks to save life will lose it, while the one who loses it for his sake will find it; this reverses the commentary's condemned preference for immediate worldly life over the life that lasts.

basis: World gained, life forfeited
note: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; the commentary likewise condemns preferring the near worldly life over the better, enduring hereafter.

basis: Eternal punishment and eternal life
note: Jesus' judgment scene ends with two enduring outcomes, punishment and life; this closely joins the commentary's fire-bound non-life to its claim that the hereafter is lasting and better.

basis: eternal punishment and eternal life
note: The final judgment divides people between eternal punishment and eternal life; its paired lasting destinies are a direct comparison for the commentary's fire and enduring afterlife.

basis: the devil offers earthly kingdoms
note: The devil offers Jesus all the kingdoms shown to him if Jesus will worship him; this is a Christian temptation scene in which the tempter offers dominion, alongside the commentary's offer of an imperishable kingdom to Adam.

basis: Earthly treasure decays
note: Jesus warns that moth, rust, and thieves undo treasure stored on earth; this gives concrete form to the commentary's near worldly life as a poor choice beside what endures.

basis: Heavenly treasure endures
note: Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven where it is not destroyed or stolen; the contrast makes explicit the commentary's preference for the better, more enduring hereafter.

basis: treasure in heaven not destroyed
note: Jesus directs disciples to treasure in heaven where decay and theft do not destroy; it translates the commentary's contrast between perishable present possession and what remains into a practice of investment.

basis: Departing to be with Christ is better
note: Paul says departure to be with Christ is far better than remaining alive; this states a specific preference for the life beyond the present one, matching the commentary's ranking of hereafter over worldly life.

basis: departure to be with Christ is far better
note: Paul calls departing to be with Christ "far better," an unusually explicit Christian comparative for the commentary's assertion that the afterlife is better than the near life.

basis: earthly-minded people have destruction as their end
note: Those whose minds are set on earthly things have destruction as their end; this makes the commentary's choice of near life into a concrete moral orientation and eschatological consequence.

basis: heavenly citizenship
note: Believers' citizenship is in heaven, giving the alternative to the preceding earthly-minded end a communal home that resonates with the commentary's enduring hereafter.

basis: fire and sulfur torment
note: The beast-worshiper is tormented with fire and sulfur, a concrete New Testament fire-punishment scene beside the commentary's fire where death does not end suffering.

basis: No rest in the judgment fire
note: The worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night under smoke of torment; this gives a specific Christian judgment image comparable to the commentary's fire without death's release, while the verse itself does not say they neither live nor die.

basis: no rest day or night, smoke forever
note: The people under judgment have no rest day or night and their torment's smoke rises forever; this specifically parallels the commentary's exclusion of sleep or a recoverable lapse in the fire.

basis: Blessed dead rest from labor
note: Revelation calls those who die in the Lord blessed and says they rest from their labors; this complicates the commentary's negated death/life condition by presenting death as a blessed rest for a different group.

basis: Tree of life in God's Paradise
note: The victor is promised fruit from the tree of life in God's Paradise; this is the positive, divinely granted counterpart to the commentary's Satanic offer of a tree of immortality.

basis: tree of life in God's paradise
note: The conqueror is granted food from the tree of life in God's paradise; this is a final Christian counterpart to the commentary's tree of immortality and its distinction between deceptive and true permanence.

basis: torment day and night forever
note: The devil, beast, and false prophet are tormented day and night for ever and ever, supplying an explicit Christian image of punitive remaining rather than release through death.

basis: Death abolished in the renewed world
note: Revelation promises that death will be no more, alongside the end of mourning and pain; unlike the commentary's fire where neither death nor life brings relief, this is death's removal within restored life.

basis: death will be no more
note: In the final renewed creation death is no more; this is the eschatological antithesis to the commentary's punitive place where death is indefinitely withheld.

basis: water of life given freely to the thirsty
note: God gives the thirsty person water from the spring of life without payment; it is a direct final-life-water analogue to the commentary's revivifying water in paradise.

basis: lake of fire identified as the second death
note: The lake burning with fire and sulfur is called the second death. The identification gives the Christian fire a death-name, in pointed contrast to 87:13's non-dying condition.

basis: River of the water of life
note: The commentary cites a Paradise water that revives what it touches; Revelation's river of the water of life flows from God's throne through the holy city, giving a precise Christian paradise-water counterpart.

basis: river of water of life in the final paradise
note: John's final city contains a river of the water of life flowing from God's throne, a directly corresponding paradise-water image for the commentary's life-giving water.

basis: Leaves for healing
note: The Paradise river's tree bears leaves for healing the nations; beside the commentary's water that revives anything it touches, Revelation depicts life-giving restoration extending through the whole blessed scene.

basis: tree of life and leaves for healing
note: Beside the river stands the tree of life whose leaves heal the nations; it brings the commentary's life-water and immortality-tree images together in the final garden.

basis: reputation of life but actual death
note: The Sardis church has a name of being alive but is dead; this non-biological use of life and death concretely parallels the commentary's definition of life by active goodness rather than mere survival.

basis: waters of life and tears removed
note: The Lamb guides the redeemed to springs of waters of life and God wipes every tear; it combines the commentary's paradise water that gives life with an eschatological relief opposite fire-torment.

basis: death sought but cannot be found
note: Under locust torment people seek death and cannot find it; like the fire-dweller of 87:13, torment continues while the normal exit of death is withheld.

basis: Death versus eternal life
note: Paul sets sin's wage, death, against God's gift of eternal life; the opposed outcomes make explicit the moral choice between death and lasting life that frames the commentary's contrast.

basis: sin's wage death, God's gift eternal life
note: Paul pairs sin's wage of death with God's gift of eternal life, a moral and eschatological life/death contrast that extends the commentary's link between life, goodness, and final outcome.

basis: eternal fire that punishes without consuming
note: Tertullian's final-judgment account treats eternal fire as ongoing punishment rather than a fire that simply consumes its victims, a patristic counterpart to the commentary's persistent fire; the precise translation should be verified.

basis: Righteous transformed to lasting glory
note: At resurrection the righteous are changed into splendor and live in an enduring order while the wicked wither; this gives apocalyptic detail to the commentary's contrast between the hereafter and the fate of those who reject it.

basis: No resurrection to life for the tyrant
note: The martyr says that for the persecuting king there will be no resurrection to life; this gives the commentary's contrast between the condemned state and lasting life a specific judgment scene.

basis: resurrection to life denied to the persecutor
note: The martyr tells the king that he will have no resurrection to life, a direct two-fate response to tyrannical violence that sharpens the commentary's contrast between punishment and the purified person's recompense.

basis: Renewal of life after death
note: A tortured brother accepts death while trusting that the King of the universe will raise him to renewed life; the scene concretely shows why the better lasting life can be preferred over survival now.

basis: tyrant's torture and everlasting renewal of life
note: A tortured brother tells the king that the King of the universe will raise the faithful to an everlasting renewal of life; like the commentary's Pharaoh-and-magicians scene, a ruler's bodily threat is answered by appeal to durable divine life.

basis: furnace of Gehenna opposite paradise of delight
note: 4 Ezra displays the furnace of Gehenna opposite the place of rest and paradise of delight, a Jewish apocalyptic pairing that makes the commentary's fire and true-life alternatives into adjacent final scenes.

basis: world to come without bodily needs, righteous enjoy divine splendor
note: The rabbinic description removes eating, drinking, and other bodily satisfactions from the world to come while the righteous enjoy divine splendor; it offers a specific Jewish construal of the commentary's true life as more than ordinary worldly vitality.

basis: Righteous living, wicked dead
note: The commentary distinguishes life as benefit and good from mere biological existence; the Talmud reads “the living know they will die” so the righteous are called living even in death and the wicked dead even while alive, turning the life/death terms into moral evaluations.

basis: righteous called living in death, wicked dead in life
note: The rabbinic maxim calls the righteous living even in death and the wicked dead even while alive; it makes life and death moral-spiritual categories, a useful interpretive comparison for the commentary's non-biological definition of life as good and benefit.

basis: This world as vestibule
note: The Mishnah pictures this world as a vestibule from which one prepares to enter the world to come; this interprets present life as provisional, clarifying why the commentary calls the hereafter the better lasting choice.

basis: this world as corridor before the world to come
note: Avot calls this world a corridor before the world to come and urges preparation here; its spatial-temporal image closely frames the commentary's near worldly life as preparatory rather than abiding.

basis: World-to-come outweighs this life
note: The Mishnah explicitly says one hour of bliss in the world to come is better than all the life of this world; this is the closest Jewish formulation of the commentary's claim that the hereafter is better and more enduring than preferred worldly life.

basis: one hour in this world and one hour in the world to come
note: Avot says both that repentance and good deeds in this world outweigh all life in the world to come and that one hour of bliss there outweighs all life here; its two-sided valuation complicates a simple worldly-life versus afterlife ranking.

basis: ordinary Gehinnom judgment limited to twelve months
note: Mishnah Eduyot limits the ordinary judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom to twelve months; that rabbinic duration qualifies the commentary's image of remaining in fire without death.

basis: shares and exclusions in the world to come
note: The mishnah grants all Israel a share in the world to come while listing exclusions; it gives a Jewish interpretive map of who receives enduring future life, relevant to the commentary's final division without claiming the same criteria.

basis: undying souls in Gehinnom
note: The Targum turns Isaiah's corpse-and-fire scene into punishment in Gehinnom in which the sinners' souls do not die, an interpretive move that closely approaches the commentary's deathless fire.

basis: God kills, makes alive, lowers and raises
note: Hannah's hymn says that the Lord kills and makes alive and brings down to Sheol and raises; it gives a fuller scriptural pattern of divine control over the two poles named in the commentary.

basis: Awakening and everlasting life
note: Daniel's sleepers in the dust awake to divergent outcomes, including everlasting life; this supplies the afterlife distinction that the commentary uses to contrast worldly life with the hereafter and its condemned endpoint.

basis: sleepers in dust awaken to enduring fates
note: Those sleeping in dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to disgrace; it makes the commentary's sleep, life, and lasting afterlife distinctions into two final outcomes rather than the suspended state of 87:13.

basis: faithful people before a king's fiery threat
note: The three Judeans tell the king that their God can rescue them from the blazing furnace and from his hand; this supplies a scriptural tyrant, fire, and faithful confession beside Pharaoh's threatened believers.

basis: everlasting dominion that will not pass away
note: The Son of Man receives a dominion that is everlasting and will not pass away; it supplies a divinely granted, genuinely imperishable rule in contrast to the commentary's satanic promise of a kingdom that does not wear out.

basis: not leaving any breathing thing alive
note: The ban commands that no breathing thing be left alive, using survival as the opposite of total extirpation; this gives a concrete Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's remaining/sparing sense of life.

basis: source label ح ي ي B013; life and good versus death and evil
note: Moses places life and good over against death and evil; Hebrew חַיִּים is cognate with the source label ح ي ي, and the explicit life/good pairing closely supports the commentary's secondary definition of life as benefit and goodness.

basis: חיים, life
note: Moses urges Israel to choose life so that they and their offspring may live; the Hebrew life cognate matches the ayah's life vocabulary, though its immediate setting is covenantal survival in the land rather than the commentary's hereafter.

basis: God kills and gives life
note: The commentary closes by citing Abraham's claim that God kills and then gives life; Deuteronomy puts that same power in God's own speech, making life and death dependent on God rather than on a ruler's threat.

basis: God kills and makes alive
note: God declares, "I kill and I make alive"; this is a direct Hebrew Bible formulation for the commentary's claim that Abraham assigns both death and life to the Lord.

basis: Living and dead as distinct states
note: Qohelet contrasts the living, who know they will die, with the dead, who know nothing; against that clean division, the commentary stresses the disturbing condition that is neither death nor beneficial life.

basis: the dead know nothing and have no further reward
note: Qohelet says the dead know nothing and no longer have reward; within its under-the-sun argument, this is a sharp Hebrew Bible counterpoint to the commentary's afterlife as the locus of true life.

basis: source label ح ي ي B006; daughters are to be kept alive
note: Pharaoh orders the midwives to kill a Hebrew son but let a daughter live; it is the biblical Pharaoh setting that makes the commentary's "leave your women alive" formula a concrete survival claim.

basis: חיה, let live
note: Pharaoh orders that every daughter be kept alive (תְּחַיּוּן); the Hebrew life verb matches the commentary's cited Arabic gloss of “let live” as “keep them alive,” including the survival sense rather than mere vitality.

basis: Egyptian magicians name God's finger while Pharaoh hardens
note: Moses' Egyptian magicians identify the plague as God's finger, but Pharaoh remains hard; the shared Moses-magicians-Pharaoh scene differs from the commentary's magicians who openly believe and receive Pharaoh's threat.

basis: God's Spirit put within the dead so they live
note: God promises to put his spirit within the restored people so that they live; this specifies divine reanimation by a life-giving force, the positive opposite of the fire's absence of life.

basis: River trees heal
note: Ezekiel's temple river nourishes trees whose leaves heal; alongside the commentary's Paradise water that revives whatever it touches, this supplies the complementary healing effect of the life-giving waterscape.

basis: River makes creatures live
note: The commentary adds the Paradise water that revives whatever it touches; Ezekiel's temple river heals its waters and makes living creatures live wherever the stream goes, a concrete life-giving-water image.

basis: water makes everything live where the river goes
note: Every living creature lives wherever Ezekiel's eschatological river goes; this is a close prophetic counterpart to the commentary's paradise water that vivifies whatever it reaches.

basis: Death warning before the serpent's claim
note: The commentary recalls Satan's offer of a tree of immortality; God first warns that eating brings death, the particular claim the serpent then denies, making this neighboring verse necessary to read the promise as counterfeit.

basis: Tree and living forever
note: The commentary calls the Satanic offer a tree of immortality and an imperishable realm; Genesis says the human might eat from the tree of life and live forever, giving the Eden scene its own guarded version of the desired permanence.

basis: חיה, live
note: Genesis uses the Hebrew life root in its statement that eating from the tree could make the human live forever; this is a direct cognate to يَحْيَىٰ in the commentary's contrast between life and death.

basis: tree of life and living forever
note: God bars the human from eating the tree of life and living forever; its actual tree-and-everlasting-life scene provides the closest biblical counterpart to the commentary's deceptive tree of immortality.

basis: The way to the life tree barred
note: After the promise of living forever, Genesis stations guardians at the way to the tree of life; this adds the scene's denial of humanly seized permanence beside the commentary's false offer of an imperishable kingdom.

basis: Serpent denies death
note: The commentary treats Satan's promise of the tree of immortality as counterfeit permanence; in Genesis the serpent directly contradicts the death warning, so the promised escape from death is itself suspect.

basis: מות, death
note: The serpent's denial uses the Hebrew root מות for dying, a concrete cognate of the ayah's يَمُوتُ; here the word is a denied consequence of eating, sharpening the contrast with the condemned person who cannot die.

basis: serpent promises no death
note: The serpent tells the woman that she will not surely die; this is the Torah's direct temptation by a denial of death beside the commentary's satanic offer of a tree of immortality.

basis: source label ب ق ي B003; preserve a remnant and keep alive
note: Joseph says God sent him ahead to preserve a remnant and keep the family alive; this joins remaining after threatened extinction to living, precisely the relation developed under the commentary's remaining/sparing branch.

basis: Ransom from Death and Sheol
note: Hosea voices Death and Sheol as powers from which Israel may be ransomed, echoing the commentary's claim that God alone gives life after death; the Hebrew can be read as a threat as well as a promise, so the connection should retain that uncertainty.

basis: Sheol and death in a disputed redemption formula
note: Hosea speaks of ransoming from Sheol and redeeming from death, but the grammar and immediate judgment context make its force disputed; its later life-over-death reception remains a cautious counterpart to the commentary's final death/life contrast.

basis: Death swallowed forever
note: Isaiah promises that God will swallow death forever and wipe away tears; this is an affirmative restoration in which death ends and life remains, a sharp contrast to the commentary's fire where neither death nor life brings relief.

basis: death swallowed forever and tears wiped away
note: God swallows up death forever and wipes tears from faces; this is a prophetic final reversal of the commentary's place where death does not provide release and true life is absent.

basis: Dead awakened to life
note: Isaiah addresses the dead as rising and waking from dust, whereas the commentary's damned person has neither death's release nor life's benefit; this is a specific prophetic reversal of that suspended fate.

basis: מות and חיה in one reversal
note: Isaiah uses cognates for “your dead” and “will live” in a single resurrection claim; the same death/life vocabulary in the ayah is here joined affirmatively rather than negated.

basis: the dead live, dust-dwellers awake
note: Isaiah calls the dead to live and the dust-dwellers to awake and sing; this eschatological reversal is the positive opposite of the commentary's fire where neither death concludes nor life begins.

basis: The living praise God
note: Hezekiah says the living, unlike those descended to the pit, give thanks to God; this concretely illustrates the commentary's gloss of life as benefit and good, though its setting is recovery from illness rather than final judgment.

basis: the living thank God
note: Hezekiah says that the living, the living give thanks to God; it makes active grateful goodness a mark of life, supporting the commentary's claim that bare survival without benefit or good is not life in the full sense.

basis: fading grass and the word standing forever
note: Grass withers and the flower fades, but God's word stands forever; this concrete transient/enduring contrast supports the commentary's evaluation of the near life against what remains.

basis: Undying worm and unquenched fire
note: The commentary describes people in fire who neither die nor live; Isaiah's closing image has the rebels' corpses exposed to a worm that does not die and fire that is not quenched, a related but carefully different image of unending judgment.

basis: corpses, undying worm, unquenched fire
note: Isaiah calls the rebels corpses, while the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched; that allocation differs from the commentary's conscious fire-inhabitant who is neither dead nor alive.

basis: death as sleep without awakening
note: A human being lies down and does not rise, not waking or being roused from sleep until the heavens are no more; Job supplies the unrecovered sleep/death image whose absence is developed in the commentary.

basis: people longing for death do not find it
note: Job describes sufferers who long for death but cannot find it; although it is not a fire judgment, it gives a specific suffering-and-unavailable-death analogue to the commentary's secondary Qur'anic comparison.

basis: source label ح ي ي B006; keep every female alive
note: Moses asks whether the women have all been kept alive; Hebrew הַחִיִּיתֶם uses the cognate life root and gives a sharply specific biblical use of the source commentary's "leaving women alive" sense.

basis: riches do not profit on the day of wrath
note: Riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death; the proverb joins the commentary's benefit-language to a final reckoning that defeats merely worldly acquisition.

basis: righteous path is life and has no death
note: The path of righteousness is life and its way has no death; this ethical use of life gives a precise Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's definition of life through good.

basis: fear of God as a fountain of life
note: The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life that turns one from death's snares; it gives an ethical-metaphorical use of life-water, distinct from the commentary's paradise-water image.

basis: death when divine breath is withdrawn
note: When God takes away creatures' breath, they die and return to dust; this concretizes the commentary's source definition of death as strength or life-force withdrawn from a thing.

basis: source label م و ت B012; sleep of death
note: The psalm asks not to sleep the sleep of death; Hebrew מָוֶת is a genuine cognate of the source label م و ت, and the verse supplies the sleep-as-death figure that the commentary says is unavailable in the fire.

basis: source label ح ي ي B013; desiring life and seeing good
note: The psalm joins desiring life with loving days in order to see good; its Hebrew life-word is cognate with ح ي ي and gives a precise biblical analogue to the commentary's life/good connection.

basis: fountain of life with God
note: The psalm calls God's presence the fountain of life; it offers a Hebrew poetic precursor for the commentary's link between life, a divine source, and life-giving water.

basis: No ransom to live forever
note: The psalm asks whether anyone can be ransomed so as to live forever without seeing the pit; against the commentary's counterfeit promise of an imperishable kingdom, it says wealth cannot secure permanence against death.

basis: living waters flow in every season
note: Living waters flow from Jerusalem both in summer and winter, an eschatological water image whose ongoing flow is a close counterpart to the commentary's paradise water and abiding life.

basis: God leads to Hades and raises
note: Wisdom says God has power over life and death, leads down to Hades and brings up again; this expands the commentary's final claim that God both causes death and gives life.

basis: humankind created for incorruption
note: Wisdom says God created humans for incorruption and made them in the image of divine eternity; it supplies a late Jewish account of true enduring life against the commentary's false promise of permanence.

basis: death enters through the devil's envy
note: Wisdom attributes death's entrance into the world to the devil's envy, a direct Jewish development of the Adam-and-tempter relation that illuminates the commentary's satanic lure of immortality.

basis: Apparent death, hope of immortality
note: The commentary rejects both death and beneficial life for the condemned; Wisdom says the righteous seemed dead to observers but are at peace and have hope full of immortality, preserving an important alternative reading of death's appearance.

basis: hope full of immortality despite apparent punishment
note: Though the righteous seem punished in human sight, their hope is full of immortality; this late Jewish reversal of apparent death and suffering closely complements the commentary's true, enduring life.
